newsitem.title: BELARUS: Thousands protest against Lukashenko in Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Thousands protest against Lukashenko in Belarus.

text.p: About 10,000 people defied a ban on marches in Belarus to protest against hardline President Alexander Lukashenko and mark Constitution Day on Saturday.
"Long live Belarus!" they shouted, showing their opposition to plans for a union with Russia which President Boris Yeltsin said on Friday could lead to a merger one day.
A resolution passed at the rally called for new elections to the parliament formed after Lukashenko won a controversial constitutional referendum on expanding his powers last November.
It also called for opposition forces to consider trying to push through early presidential elections.
"Fascism! Lukashism!" protesters chanted after police blocked them from proceeding down the central avenue of the capital Minsk, where Lukashenko's residence is situated.
Instead police with riot gear and truncheons funnelled the crowds down side-streets. Marching had been officially banned.
On Friday, police used truncheons to break up a rally of up to 2,000 young activists and arrested about 100 people, including two Americans, two Germans and several journalists.

But on Saturday protesters made their way to an area near the Palace of Sports where opposition politicians denounced Lukashenko's amended version of the former Soviet republic's constitution. The original was written four years ago.
The Popular Front, the most active opposition group whose 53-year-old leader was arrested in a late-night police raid on Thursday, said seven protesters were arrested.

The referendum, widely discredited since Lukashenko ignored the constitutional court, parliament and the constitution itself to push it through, gave him wide authority over all branches of power and allowed him to recommence his five-year term.
This will give him a total of 7-1/2 years at the helm of the state on Russia's western border whose identity is intimately tied up with Moscow after centuries of Russian and Soviet rule.

Lukashenko praised his new constitution as a "guarantor of domestic political stability" in an address in official newspapers. "The updated constitution created a foundation for fulfilling the individual's rights and freedom," it said.
Saturday's rally was led by Semyon Sharetsky, speaker of the old parliament who led attempts to stop the November polls.

"Under cover of the so-called referendum, a coup d'etat has taken place in Belarus. Its organiser, spiritual leader and manager was Alexander Lukashenko, who brutally violated the old constitution," Sharetsky told the crowds.
Youngsters ripped up official Belarussian flags which had been put up for the holiday. Lukashenko revived the Soviet-era flag in place of the red-and-white one adopted on independence.
Earlier this month the president banned the display of post-independence symbols as part of a crackdown on opposition forces who have promised him a "political spring".
Lukashenko is backed by most of the 10 million Belarussians but is opposed by a loose union of liberals, nationalists, intellectuals and students mostly concentrated in Minsk.
Some 60 deputies who refused to join the new parliament met on Friday night to call on the outside world not to recognise Lukashenko's new constitution and to mark Constitution Day.
They were joined by the German ambassador, Italian charge d'affaires and British and Russian embassy officials.
The United States said on Friday it had downgraded its relationship with Belarus because of what it called a "serious turn for the worse" in the human rights situation.
